notes.shape: The yield curve plots Treasury yields from short maturities (1 month) to long maturities (30 years), with an upward slope indicating normal economic conditions and a downward (inverted) slope historically preceding recessions by 6-18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.69%, and the 10-year minus 2-year (2s10s) spread is 0.34 percentage points, indicating a positive slope. This contrasts with the 2022-2024 period when the 2s10s spread was inverted (below zero) for an extended duration. The recent shift to a positive spread marks a re-steepening of the curve above zero after the deepest inversion reached 0.0 points in the data series.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread serves as a leading recession indicator; an inverted spread historically signals economic downturn risk. The extended inversion from 2022 through 2024 suggested heightened recession risks, but the recent positive spread of 0.34 points implies a partial normalization of market expectations. However, the New York Fed's recession probability model still assigns a 31% chance of recession, underscoring ongoing uncertainty. It is important to note that the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before recessions, so a positive slope does not eliminate recession risk.
notes.now: The current positive 2s10s spread and elevated 10-year yield indicate improved economic sentiment relative to the prior inversion period. Nevertheless, with a 31% recession probability from the NY Fed model, the yield curve signals caution without confirming imminent recession. The data reflect an uncertain outlook where the market is no longer signaling imminent contraction through inversion, but risk remains present.
